WHO Guidelines for the Treatment of Treponema pallidum (Syphilis): The global prevalence and incidence of Chlamydia trachomatis infections remain high, with nearly one million new curable infections occurring daily. These infections can lead to acute conditions such as cervicitis, urethritis, and genital ulceration. The 2003 WHO guidelines recommend treating uncomplicated anogenital infections with either doxycycline (100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days) or azithromycin (1 g orally as a single dose). Alternative regimens include amoxicillin (500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days), erythromycin (500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days), ofloxacin (300 mg orally twice daily for 7 days), or tetracycline (500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days). Assessment of Anorectal Chlamydia Infections: There is no global prevalence data for anorectal Chlamydia trachomatis infections. Rectal infections are rarely tested and often occur concurrently with genital infections. In 2012, an estimated 131 million new cases of Chlamydia were reported globally, with approximately 128 million cases among adults aged 15–49 years. These infections can result in severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and neonatal complications such as premature delivery and severe disability. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of treating anorectal infections due to their potential to cause vaginal reinfection, which can perpetuate the infection within the community. Antimicrobial resistance data should also be considered, although research in this area is limited. Treatment Comparisons: Evidence from studies suggests that doxycycline may result in approximately 200 fewer cures per 1,000 cases compared to azithromycin, with little-to-no difference in side effects. However, the WHO panel emphasized the importance of treating women, as they are more likely to be tested for genital infections but not for anal infections, despite the serious long-term consequences.
